extracted.intended_audience: prospective applicants and campus sponsored programs or grants officers at public higher education institutions
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for higher-education institutions on identifying appropriate private foundations and preparing letters of inquiry and formal proposals for foundation grants. Covers research, campus coordination, proposal contents, budgeting (including indirect costs), timing, and follow-up after decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness for foundation funding
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask, 'Is this project appropriate for foundation funding?' Most foundations will only fund special projects or provide start-up support for activities that will become self-sustaining after a short period of time; they prefer projects on the 'cutting edge' and seldom support projects that can be funded easily through state and federal mechanisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foundations leverage limited resources for greatest impact—seek funding for novel approaches to social problems, short-term start-ups, demonstrations, or activities unlikely to be financed by government. If the project can be readily supported by state/federal funds, don't target private foundations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand foundation type and funding patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize differences among Independent (local vs. national), Company/Corporate-Sponsored, Community (public) foundations, and Operating foundations—each has specific funding patterns and priorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local independent foundations primarily fund nearby/community-benefitting projects; national foundations may fund riskier, replicable projects; corporate foundations fund areas related to company activities and local communities; community foundations focus on local needs and capital support; operating foundations seldom make external grants. Match project scope and geography to type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider foundation staffing and review style
rubrics_metrics.description: Foundation staffing (bank trusts, volunteer boards, or professional staff) affects applicant interaction and proposal review; large foundations often have program officers who counsel applicants, while many operate without paid staff and have limited advance contact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a foundation has program staff, use them for advice during proposal development; for foundations without staff, rely on external research and colleagues' experience. Expect variance in responsiveness and guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal/tax constraints affecting foundation behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Foundations are tax-exempt under Section 501(c)(3) and subject to Internal Revenue Code rules (e.g., must pay out at least 5 percent of annual investment income and pay excise tax on net investment income).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These regulatory and tax requirements constrain foundation practices and may influence grantmaking priorities and payout behavior; be aware that foundations can change program direction freely within those boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use directories and initial research (exploring possibilities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop a list of foundations that have demonstrated interest in your project area and that support organizations in your geographic region using directories such as The Foundation Directory, Source Book Profiles, and the Taft Foundation Reporter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read directory descriptions and ask: Do goals match the foundation's priorities? Does it give to public institutions? Does it support projects in this geography and this project type (research, demonstration, service)? Does it provide the funding type needed (seed, endowment, construction)? Is grant range and period in line with your budget? Eliminate foundations that don't match to conserve effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review actual grant listings to narrow prospects
rubrics_metrics.description: Because priorities may be broadly stated, review listings of grants actually made (e.g., Foundation Grants Index) to identify a foundation's true priorities and patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for geographic concentration, favored project types (e.g., endowments vs. program support), and typical award sizes. Remove foundations whose real giving patterns do not match your needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtain current foundation materials and contacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Directories may be 2–3 years old; request annual reports, application guidelines, or policy statements directly from foundations if available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contact the foundation's public relations or communications officer for current information; if materials aren't published, consult the nearest Foundation Center Cooperative Reference Collection for Form 990-PF and updated information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult colleagues and campus experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Talk to people on your campus or in your field who have worked with the foundation to gain insight into priorities and practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Colleagues' firsthand experience can reveal unstated preferences, indirect cost policies, and practical tips for successful proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate submissions across campus
rubrics_metrics.description: Work with your campus-sponsored programs or grants officer to determine whether the university already has a proposal pending with the foundation and to notify other campus offices of your submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordination prevents duplicate solicitations while a proposal is active and helps administrators allocate institutional resources effectively. The sponsored programs office typically coordinates campus-wide external funding efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secure institutional commitment and senior endorsement
rubrics_metrics.description: Most foundations will not accept a proposal without the endorsement of a senior university official and commitment of institutional resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foundations view institutional endorsement and committed resources as evidence of management capacity; absence of coordination may signal poor project management and jeopardize all proposals from the institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letter of inquiry (initial contact) content and format
rubrics_metrics.description: Many foundations use a two-stage process starting with a brief letter of inquiry (usually no longer than two to three pages) describing the project, plan of action, background of key personnel, tentative budget, and the purpose of the organization. The first paragraph should contain a brief description of the project and the amount requested—not a description of the organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate knowledge of the foundation and a clear connection between its work and your project; outline significance, who benefits, and an indication of step-by-step planning. Keep the LOI concise; avoid mass mailings (which can damage credibility); if soliciting multiple foundations, inform program officers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal proposal match and review questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Program officers first determine whether the project fits the foundation's specific priorities and then ask: Will the project make a difference? Does the project tackle too much? Is the budget request sound? Is there institutional commitment? Is the evaluation plan sound?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the project 'makes sense,' is well thought out, clear in purpose, and unique. Align proposal emphasis with the foundation's priorities and be prepared to answer these central evaluative questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal proposal recommended structure and length
rubrics_metrics.description: If the foundation does not provide specific guidelines, prepare a formal proposal approximately ten pages in length including a one-page summary/precis, institutional description and authorized signature, body with rationale, objectives, implementation schedule, evaluation, qualifications, proof of tax-exempt status, and a project budget with future funding plans for multiyear projects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include: (1) a summary letter or one-page precis stating purpose, amount requested, and expected time period; (2) description of your institution and signature of an authorized official; (3) body: rationale/needs statement, description of target population, four or five measurable objectives, implementation schedule, plans for evaluation; (4) description of personnel qualifications; (5) proof of tax-exempt status; (6) project budget including future funding plans and evidence of direct cost sharing by the university/other groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define measurable objectives and evaluation plans
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal proposals should contain four or five measurable objectives and plans for evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objectives should be specific and measurable; evaluation plans must be sound and demonstrate how impact will be assessed—foundations weigh evaluation in their decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personnel qualifications and institutional capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a description of the qualifications of the personnel involved in the project and evidence of the institution's capacity to carry out the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foundations review applicant institutions as well as project structure and objectives; demonstrating capable personnel and institutional support increases likelihood of funding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of tax-exempt status
rubrics_metrics.description: Include proof of the university's tax-exempt status as required by the Internal Revenue Code.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foundations require this documentation as a standard component of formal proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budgeting and indirect cost (overhead) strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Foundations vary widely in allowing indirect costs: many do not support any indirect costs, few will allow the full government overhead rate, and some will provide a portion. Foundations developed these positions because reimbursing indirect costs reduces the number of grants that can be made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategies: (a) apply your full federal indirect rate in the proposed budget but agree to cover all but 5–15 percent of those costs yourself; (b) reclassify items normally in indirect costs (rent, equipment use, administrative salaries) into direct cost line items selectively; (c) consult program officers or colleagues for a foundation's policy; (d) leave indirect-cost questions out of the LOI phase and address them if asked in the full proposal; (e) ensure administration is aware, because unrecovered indirect costs draw on institutional resources; (f) include substantial direct cost sharing in the budget.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and board meeting schedules
rubrics_metrics.description: Grant decisions are often tied to foundation board meetings, which may occur as infrequently as once or twice a year; foundations need to receive applications at least two to three months in advance of board meetings to allow time for review and investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check directories for board meeting months or frequency and plan submissions accordingly so applications are received in time for consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding to rejection and resubmission practices
rubrics_metrics.description: If a proposal is turned down, find out why and ask for suggestions to improve the presentation. Do not resubmit without making substantive changes according to the foundation's concerns; successful proposals are usually the result of multiple submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The extent of debriefing depends on foundation staff size; use any feedback to revise and strengthen your proposal before resubmitting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start early and allow time for research and revision
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin the search long before you actually need the money. Thorough research of potential sponsors and sufficient time to develop concise letters of inquiry and proposals will enhance chances for success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow time for iterative drafting, coordination with campus offices, obtaining institutional endorsements, and aligning submission timing with foundation review cycles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Foundation Center resources and Cooperating Collections
rubrics_metrics.description: The Foundation Center provides comprehensive information, directories, databases, and reference collections; Cooperating Collections (libraries, community foundations) provide access to Foundation Center publications and many have sets of private foundation information returns (IRS Form 990-PF).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage Foundation Center publications (Foundation Directory, Source Book Profiles, Foundation Grants Index, etc.), Comsearch printouts, and local Cooperating Collections for detailed, up-to-date information and Form 990-PF returns. Call collections in advance to confirm hours and holdings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mass mailings; disclose multiple solicitations
rubrics_metrics.description: A mass mailing can damage your credibility. If soliciting several different foundations, inform program officers that you have approached other potential funders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program officers appreciate transparency and may coordinate joint funding if interested; targeted, researched solicitations are more credible than generic mass mailings.
